prompt: A blob is deleted in an account with blob soft delete set to 14 days. What happens on day 5?
hint: Nothing moved; it is marked.

choices.text: It is gone, and only a backup can bring it back
choices.why: That is the account without soft delete.

choices.text: It sits in a recycle-bin container you can browse
choices.why: Nothing is moved; the blob stays under its own name, marked deleted.

choices.text: Kept, marked deleted, and billed until day 14
choices.why: Right. After day 14 it is gone for good.

choices.text: The delete was refused, because the blob is protected for 14 days
choices.why: Soft delete never stops a delete; that is immutability.

prompt: An engineer deletes the whole `orders-raw` container by mistake. Blob soft delete is on; container soft delete is off. What can be recovered?
hint: The two switches protect against different mistakes.

choices.text: Nothing; that needed the other switch
choices.why: Right. The two are independent switches.

choices.text: Every blob, because blob soft delete covers them
choices.why: Blob soft delete covers blobs deleted one by one, not a deleted container.

choices.text: The container, empty, since only blobs were soft deleted
choices.why: Without container soft delete the container is gone too.

choices.text: The blobs written in the last 14 days
choices.why: Retention counts from the deletion, not from when blobs were written.

prompt: What is the longest blob soft-delete retention, in days, that the Terraform provider accepted?
hint: The refusal printed the range.

prompt: In a versioned account, a program deletes `rates/usd-brl.csv`. What is left?
hint: A delete with versioning destroys nothing.

choices.text: Nothing; versioning only protects overwrites
choices.why: A delete turns the current content into a previous version.

choices.text: The blob, unchanged, because deletes are refused while versioning is on
choices.why: Nothing refuses the delete; only immutability does that.

choices.text: A soft-deleted blob that disappears after the retention days
choices.why: That is soft delete without versioning.

choices.text: A previous version holding its content
choices.why: Right. Restoring is a copy, which is itself a new version.

prompt: A 50 GB table is rewritten whole every night in a versioned account with no rule for versions. Roughly how many GB of previous versions does it hold after 365 nights?
hint: Each night leaves one full copy behind.

prompt: In `snapshot.py`, how was the right exchange rate restored?
hint: The last two lines of the program.

choices.text: By deleting the current blob, so the snapshot took its place
choices.why: A snapshot never replaces its base on its own.

choices.text: By copying the snapshot's URL over the blob's own name
choices.why: Right, the same way a version is restored.

choices.text: By an undelete of the snapshot
choices.why: Nothing was deleted, and Azurite has no undelete.

choices.text: By renaming the snapshot to the blob's name
choices.why: Blob Storage has no rename, as lesson 3 counted.

prompt: What is the difference between a snapshot and a version?
hint: Who decides when each one is made?

choices.text: A snapshot is writable and a version is read-only
choices.why: Both are read-only copies.

choices.text: A version is made on every write; a snapshot only when a program asks
choices.why: Right. Versioning automates what snapshots did by hand.

choices.text: Snapshots are free, versions are billed
choices.why: Both keep data that is billed.

choices.text: Versions survive a delete, snapshots are deleted with the blob first
choices.why: That is not what separates them; who triggers them is.

prompt: In `lifecycle.tf`, why does `prefix_match` start with `orders-raw/`?
hint: A rule belongs to the account, not to one container.

choices.text: It is a folder the rule creates for moved blobs
choices.why: A rule creates nothing; it moves and deletes.

choices.text: Prefixes must start with the account's name
choices.why: The account is implied; the prefix starts with the container.

choices.text: It is optional decoration; the rule applies to the whole account
choices.why: Without it the rule would apply to every block blob in the account.

choices.text: It names the container first, then the start of the blob names
choices.why: Right. So the rule touches the exports and nothing else in the account.

prompt: Why does Quitanda's rule for the exports stop at cold instead of archive?
hint: Which account are the exports in, and how is it replicated?

choices.text: Its account is ZRS, a replication with no such tier
choices.why: Right, as lesson 4 found.

choices.text: Cold is cheaper than archive for data kept seven years
choices.why: Archive keeps a gigabyte for less; the reason is elsewhere.

choices.text: A rule cannot move blobs to archive
choices.why: The provider listed `tier_to_archive_...` actions.

choices.text: Archive would break the versions rule
choices.why: Versions have archive actions of their own.

prompt: A colleague proposes a rule that moves logs to cold at 30 days and deletes them at 60. What does every log cost?
hint: Lesson 4's minimums apply to what a rule does.

choices.text: 30 days of hot and 30 of cold, as written
choices.why: Cold's minimum is 90 days and is billed in full.

choices.text: Nothing extra, since rules are exempt from early deletion
choices.why: There is no such exemption.

choices.text: 30 days of hot and 90 of cold, 60 of them for days it did not stay
choices.why: Right. A rule knows nothing about minimum days.

choices.text: The rule is refused, because 60 is less than cold's minimum
choices.why: Nothing checks the rule against the minimums; the bill does.

prompt: A life-cycle rule is saved at 14:00. When does Microsoft document that it starts moving blobs?
hint: The policy is not instant.

choices.text: At once, for every blob that matches
choices.why: Policies are run by the platform once a day, not on save.

choices.text: At 14:00 the next day exactly
choices.why: There is no fixed hour; it is up to 24 hours, then the time the actions take.

choices.text: After 30 days, the shortest age in the rule
choices.why: The ages are the blobs', not the rule's.

choices.text: Within about 24 hours, and its actions take longer on a large account
choices.why: Right. A rule written today archives nothing tonight.

prompt: Match each protection to what it does.
hint: Two keep a copy after the mistake, two refuse it.

pairs.right: keeps a deleted blob for some days
refuses changes until it is cleared

prompt: Why does `audit.tf` set `locked = false` in its first version?
hint: What can be undone on a locked policy?

choices.text: Locked policies are not supported on ZRS accounts
choices.why: The lesson names no such limit.

choices.text: Terraform cannot create a locked policy
choices.why: `locked` is an attribute the provider accepts as `true` too.

choices.text: So the design is tested first; locked, it only grows
choices.why: Right. Locking is a reviewed change made once everyone agrees.

choices.text: An unlocked policy refuses deletes for longer
choices.why: Both refuse for the same period; only the locked one cannot be shortened.

prompt: A lawsuit requires Quitanda to keep September's invoices unchanged until it ends, a date nobody knows. Which protection fits?
hint: One of them has no date.

choices.text: A time-based retention of seven years, to be safe
choices.why: It fixes a date nobody chose, and a locked one cannot be shortened if the case ends early.

choices.text: A legal hold, cleared when the case ends
choices.why: Right. It lasts as long as it lasts.

choices.text: Soft delete with the maximum of 365 days
choices.why: Soft delete lets the change happen; the case needs it refused.

choices.text: Versioning, so every change is kept
choices.why: It keeps changes rather than refusing them.

prompt: Azurite stored a soft-delete policy of 7 days. What did the listing with `--include d` show after a delete?
hint: The setting answered as if it worked.

choices.text: An empty list
choices.why: Right. The setting was stored and nothing was kept.

choices.text: The deleted blob, with `deleted: true`
choices.why: That is what Azure would show for seven days.

choices.text: An error, because `--include d` is not supported
choices.why: The listing answered without complaint, with nothing in it.

choices.text: The blob, still current, because Azurite ignored the delete
choices.why: The delete worked; the blob was simply gone.

prompt: What does `APINotImplemented` from Azurite tell you?
hint: Read the message that came with it.

choices.text: That the request was malformed and should be fixed
choices.why: The same request works on Azure; it is the emulator that lacks it.

choices.text: That the account needs a login first
choices.why: That is the control-plane message, `Please run 'az login'`.

choices.text: That Azurite has not written that operation
choices.why: Right. The message says so plainly.

choices.text: That the feature is switched off for this account
choices.why: Nothing about the account was switched off; the message says the operation is not written.

prompt: Which of these does a passing test against Azurite prove? Choose all that apply.
hint: Only what Azurite actually did, rather than stored or refused.

choices.text: That a snapshot is kept and can be copied back over the blob
choices.why: Yes; Azurite implements snapshots.

choices.text: That a deleted blob can be undeleted within the retention
choices.why: Azurite kept nothing and refused the undelete.

choices.text: That the soft-delete request is well formed
choices.why: Yes, and nothing more.

choices.text: That a stored version id restores the right content
choices.why: Azurite gave no version ids at all.

prompt: Order the protections from the one that only keeps a deleted blob for a while to the one nobody can undo.
hint: Soft delete is first; a locked policy is last.

prompt: In a life-cycle rule, the `blob_types` value for block blobs is spelt `___`.
hint: Lower case first, then a capital.

prompt: Which protection would have saved the six log lines that lesson 2's `--overwrite` destroyed, with nothing else switched on?
hint: An overwrite, not a delete.

choices.text: Versioning
choices.why: Right. The overwrite would have left the six lines as a previous version.

choices.text: Container soft delete
choices.why: Nobody deleted the container.

choices.text: A life-cycle rule
choices.why: A rule moves and deletes by age; it keeps nothing.

choices.text: A legal hold set after the overwrite
choices.why: It would protect the new content, not the lost one.

prompt: Quitanda's audit records must not be changed for seven years, and an auditor will ask how that is guaranteed. Which design answers?
hint: Keeping a copy is not the same as refusing the change.

choices.text: Versioning, with a life-cycle rule that keeps every version for seven years
choices.why: Anybody allowed to delete versions can still delete them.

choices.text: Soft delete at its maximum, renewed every year
choices.why: 365 days is the maximum, and it never refuses a change.

choices.text: A tested restore procedure from Azurite snapshots
choices.why: Azurite is a lab; it guarantees nothing about Azure.

choices.text: A locked seven-year retention on a container that holds only the records
choices.why: Right. Nobody can shorten it, and nothing else is locked in with it.
